# Introduction

BioBead is a biodegradable hydrogel pellet containing fungal and
bacterial consortia for soil health and regenerative agriculture.
Microbes in this consortia can fix nitrogen (N), solubilize phosphorus
(P), and drive carbon (C) cycling. Arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF)
are obligate mutualists that make direct contact with plant roots and
hand off N and P to plants, obtaining C in return. They also provide
structures for microbial residence and travel. Greenhouse studies with
BioBead have demonstrated improved growth for tomatoes and wheat plants,
increases in soil organic matter, and promotion of closed nutrient
cycling.

In 2025, a greenhouse study led by Renee Davis and Korena Mafune, PhD
evaluated the impacts of 14 different microbe inoculations and
treatments on soil microbiology, wheat growth, root colonization, and
greenhouse gas emissions. This specific project will focus on soil
geochemistry, nutrient dynamics, and soil moisture data, with other data
being incorporated in subsequent phases. The responses measured at
different intervals will have to be analyzed separately, or combined in
another manner. These results will provide a foundation for expansion
into larger field trials and BioBead formulation improvements in 2026
and beyond, and hopefully become publications and dissertation chapters.

## Research Questions

1.  Does the hydrogel carrier in BioBead explain variation in the soil
    geochemical profile and wheat yield?

2.  How does the interaction of the hydrogel and microbes explain
    variation in the soil geochemical profile and wheat yield?

3.  What are the principle components driving variation in these
    multivariate soil responses?

# Methods

## Greenhouse Trial and Sample Collection

Wheat seedlings (Red Fife variety, Territorial Seeds) were planted in
1-gallon pots containing sunshine mix and sand (1:2 v/v) from
September-December 2025 at the UW Biology Greenhouse. The experiment
utilized a randomized design with 14 treatments and 7 biological
replicates per treatment (98 pots total). Microbial inoculants were
applied at planting according to treatment specifications.

Plants were grown for 14 weeks under greenhouse conditions. Plants were
watered weekly with 200 mL water, and soil moisture was recorded 24
hours after each watering event. Leachate samples were collected at
weeks 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 and analyzed using The Gallery (ThermoFisher) for
ammonium, nitrate, and phosphate concentrations.

Plant Root Simulator (PRS) Probes (Western Ag Innovations) were buried
at week 6 and retrieved after 14 days. Probes were sent to Western Ag
for analysis of soil cation and anion exchange capacity via HPLC. At
experiment termination (week 14), above-ground biomass was harvested and
weighed, and rhizosphere soil and root samples were collected and stored
at -80°C for future DNA extraction and metagenomic sequencing. (These
data are mentioned for reference and will not be analyzed in this
project.)

# Data

## Files

**2025biobeadgreenhouse.Rmd** - R Markdown file containing this
document.

The data are compiled into a single spreadsheet
(**2025greenhousemaster.csv**), which can be found in the [GitHub
repository](https://github.com/reneeadeledavis/biobead). It was compiled
from the following raw data.

-   **Leachates_2025.csv** - Ammonium, nitrate, and phosphate leachate
    concentrations recorded throughout the study.

-   **PRS_GH_2025.csv** - Soil anion and cation exchange data from PRS
    probes.

-   **WheatMoistureData_2025.csv** - Soil moisture data recorded
    throughout the study.

**N2O_flux.data.csv** - Nitrous oxide (N2O) flux was also calculated.
The data are limited to 3 replicates per treatment (not 7), so these
data will remain in its own file rather than grafted to the master
spreadsheet.

**Wheat yield data** has been added to the master spreadsheet, and
includes 2 columns on grain yield (per sample unit) and an associated
Harvest Index (HI), which is a ratio of grain yield over the rest of the
above-ground biomass. It represents an economically-relevant measure of
wheat crop productivity.

Exploratory one-way ANOVAs have already been performed on
[leachate](https://rpubs.com/reneedavis/1389304), [soil
moisture](https://rpubs.com/reneedavis/moisture2025), [anion/cation
supply rate](https://rpubs.com/reneedavis/ions2025), [wheat
yield](https://rpubs.com/reneedavis/wheatyield2025), and [N2O
flux](https://rpubs.com/reneedavis/1392995).

## Treatment codes

T1 - BioBead – bacteria

T2 - BioBead – AMF

T3 - BioBead - bacteria, AMF

T4 - SL-primed BioBead - bacteria, AMF

T5 - SL-primed BioBead - bacteria

T6 - SL-primed BioBead - AMF

T7 - BioBead w/ reapplication at week 8

T8 - ½ fertilizer ½ BioBead

T9 - Liquid consortia

T10 - Commercial biofertilizer (Hardygro)

T11 - Empty bead

T12 - SL-primed empty bead

T13 - Synthetic fertilizer (positive control – 10% dose, 0.6 g/L,
10mL/pot)

T14 - Untreated

Specific replicates of samples are indicated after a dash in the sample
code. For example, certain replicates in the PRS data are designated as
T1-1, T1-2, T1-3, etc.

# Exploratory NMDS

Nonmetric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) was used to visualize
multivariate treatment effects across two datasets: a master dataset
comprising nutrient leachate (NH₄-N, NO₃-N, PO₄-P), soil moisture, and
wheat yield metrics (grain weight, harvest index); and a soil ion
dataset comprising 15 ion supply rates measured by Plant Root Simulator
(PRS) probes (NO₃-N, NH₄-N, P, Ca, Mg, K, Fe, Mn, Cu, Zn, B, S, Pb, Al,
Cd, Na). Prior to ordination, all variables were relativized by column
maxima using the `decostand` function to account for differences in
scale across the different response variables. Euclidean distances were
used and NMDS was performed in three dimensions for the master dataset
and two dimensions for the ion dataset using `metaMDS` with 100 random
starts. Ordination stress was evaluated to confirm adequate fit.
Treatment groups were visualized using convex hull ellipses via the
`ggforce` package in R (version 4.5.2), with treatments colored by
inoculant class: core BioBead formulations (blues), strigolactone-primed
BioBead formulations (greens), bead-only controls (purples), and
reference treatments including synthetic fertilizer, liquid consortia,
commercial biofertilizer, and untreated negative control.

## Soil Properties NMDS

```{r}
library(vegan)
library(dplyr)

# load in data
data <- read.csv("2025greenhousemaster_hydrogel.csv", header = TRUE, row.names = 1)
ions <- read.csv("ions/PRS_2025_hydrogel.csv", header = TRUE)

# Subset response and explanatory variables
treatments <- data$Treatment_Category
soil_properties <- data[ , !colnames(data) %in% "Treatment_Category"]
soil_properties_rel <- decostand(soil_properties, method = "max") ## Relativize by column maxima

# create Euclidean distance matrix
data_dist <- vegdist(soil_properties_rel, method = "euclidean")

set.seed(1)
nmds_result <- metaMDS(soil_properties_rel, 
                       distance = "euclidean", 
                       k = 3, 
                       trymax = 100)
nmds_result$stress

#create data frame
cluster_df <- data.frame( 
  label = rownames(data),
  cluster = as.factor(data$Treatment_Category)
)
head(cluster_df)

nmds_scores <- vegan::scores(nmds_result, tidy = TRUE) |> 
  filter(score == "sites") |> 
  left_join(cluster_df, by = "label")

# color palette 
treatment_colors <- c(
  "BioBead"           = "#CDEE40FF",  # yellow-green

  "Hydrogel"              = "#8BD4F7FF",  # grey
  "Microbe_Liquid"            = "#E96C0CFF",  # red-orange
  "Negative"                = "#000000"   # black (negative control)
)

#plot
library(ggplot2)
p1 <- ggplot(nmds_scores, aes(x = NMDS1, y = NMDS2, colour = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = treatment_colors, name = "Treatment Group") +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = cluster), level = 0.95, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +  # potentially correct to ggforce (below), this assumes normal dist
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "NMDS1", y = "NMDS2",
       caption = "Figure 1: NMDS Ordination of Leachate, Soil Moisture, and Wheat Yield")

p1
```

Based on the ordination, there is no apparent strong multivariate
separation between treatments. The fertilizer and liquid consortia
(liquid_mixed) is the most distant, indicating that it had unique
effects on the response variables. The ellipses are also large,
indicating that the variability within the group is high. The BioBead
treatments (blue group) have tighter ellipses. This means that they are
producing more consistent responses in leachate, soil moisture, and
wheat yield.

## Soil Ion NMDS

```{r}
library(tidyr)
# Load data
ions <- read.csv("ions/PRS_2025_hydrogel.csv", header = TRUE, row.names = 1)

# Subset
ions_treatments <- ions$Treatment_Category
ions_properties <- ions[ , !colnames(ions) %in% "Treatment_Category"]
ions_rel <- decostand(ions_properties, method = "max")

# Create Euclidean distance matrix
ions_dist <- vegdist(ions_rel, method = "euclidean")

# NMDS
set.seed(1)
nmds_ions <- metaMDS(ions_dist,
                     k = 2,
                     trymax = 100)
nmds_ions$stress

#create data frame
cluster_df_ions <- data.frame( 
  label = rownames(ions),
  cluster = as.factor(ions$Treatment_Category)
)
head(cluster_df_ions)

nmds_scores_ions <- vegan::scores(nmds_ions, tidy = TRUE) |> 
  filter(score == "sites") |> 
  left_join(cluster_df_ions, by = "label")

library(ggforce)
p2 <- ggplot(nmds_scores_ions, aes(x = NMDS1, y = NMDS2, colour = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = treatment_colors, name = "Treatment Group") +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = cluster), level = 0.95, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "NMDS1", y = "NMDS2",
       caption = "Figure 2: NMDS Ordination of Soil Ion Supply Rates by Treatment")
p2
```

The ion ordination was also a generally good fit for the original data
(stress 0.111). It shows a slightly different story than the previous
ordination. Here, the BioBead treatments have larger ellipses,
highlighting more within-group variability. Fertilizer and liquid_mixed
are tighter. The strigolactone (SL) primed treatments are pulling to the
upper left of the ordination space, and are clustering together. This
generally shows that soil ions have different patterning than the other
3 response variables in regards to treatment categories.

# Hydrogel influences on soil physiochemical properties

## Soil physiochemical properties

The analysis of hydrogel influences will take place in 2 parts: the soil
physiochemical properties (leachate, moisture, wheat yield) and soil
ions.

### PERMANOVA

First, I will conduct a PERMANOVA on a select number of treatment
categories:

1.  T3 - BioBead - bacteria, AMF
2.  T9 - Liquid consortia
3.  T11 - Empty bead
4.  T14 - Negative control

The hypothesis is that there are differences in soil physiochemical
properties for these different treatment groups. Permutations not
restricted, as the study utilized a randomized block design so there are
no bench effects to account for.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
gel_permanova_result <- adonis2(data_dist ~ treatments, 
                                permutations = 9999)
gel_permanova_result
```

In this test, the treatment group explained 32.8% of the multivariate
variance (R² = 0.328), with a highly significant F statistic (F = 4.386,
p = 0.0001). This confirms the hypothesis that there are differences in
soil physiochemical properties in these different treatment groups.

Practically, these data mean that the 3 treatment groups produce
meaningfully different multivariate soil/yield profiles. These three
treatments isolate the carrier and microbial effects, so the separation
suggests the hydrogel carrier and microbial consortia are each
contributing something distinct rather than being interchangeable.

### Two-Factor PERMANOVA

I can use the approach of a two-factor PERMANOVA to understand how much
variance is captured by the presence or absence of the hydrogel, the
presence or absence of the microbes, and the interaction between the
two. In order to do this, I manually created 2 additional columns in the
data files in Excel to indicate hydrogel Y/N and microbe Y/N. Treatments
were coded with hydrogels and microbes even if present in small amounts
(e.g. BioBead_Mixed_Reduced, HalfF_HalfBB). Hardygro was marked as
present for microbe.

```{r}
data_gel2factor <- read.csv("2025greenhousemaster_gel2factor.csv", header = TRUE, row.names = 1)

# Subset 
soil_properties <- data_gel2factor[ , !colnames(data_gel2factor) %in% c("Treatment_Category", "Hydrogel", "Microbe")]

# Relativize/redo distance matrix
soil_properties_rel <- decostand(soil_properties, method = "max")
gel2factor_dist <- vegdist(soil_properties_rel, method = "euclidean")

set.seed(1)
gel_permanova_2way <- adonis2(
  gel2factor_dist ~ Hydrogel * Microbe,
  data = data_gel2factor,
  permutations = 9999,
  by = "term"
)
gel_permanova_2way
```

The hydrogel accounts for 13.9% of the variance in the responses (F =
8.4106, p = 0.0001). The presence or absence of microbe accounts for
9.8% of the variance and is also highly significant (F = 5.9437, p =
0.0001). Together, their interaction accounts for 2% of the variance but
is not statistically significant (F = 1.1914, p = 0.3069). The R2 from
Hydrogel, Microbe, and their interaction is 0.25676, meaning that these
factors can explain 25.7% of the multivariate response.

### RDA

Following this PERMANOVA test, a redundancy analysis (RDA) can help
visualize what treatments drive separation of responses.

```{r}
gel_rda <- rda(
  soil_properties_rel ~ Hydrogel * Microbe,
  data = data_gel2factor,
  scale = FALSE  
)

summary(gel_rda)

# Significance test of the full model
anova(gel_rda, permutations = 9999)

anova(gel_rda, by = "term", permutations = 9999)

# Plot
plot(gel_rda, type = "n")
points(gel_rda, display = "sites", 
       col = treatment_colors[data_gel2factor$Treatment_Category], 
       pch = 16, cex = 1.2)
text(gel_rda, display = "bp", col = "#1927DDFF")  # arrows for explanatory variables
legend("topright", legend = names(treatment_colors), 
       col = treatment_colors, pch = 16, cex = 0.7)
mtext("Figure 3: RDA of Soil and Yield Properties constrained by Hydrogel and Microbe presence", 
      side = 1, # bottom of plot
      line = 4, # how far below the axis
      cex = 0.8) # font size
```

<!--# RDA axis breakdown - update this section -->

From this RDA, we can see a few trends. The Hydrogel (Y) arrow points to
the upper left, and so does the interaction arrow (Hydrogel Y/Microbe
Y). This means that the interaction is largely due to the hydrogel
signal. The BioBead treatments (blue dots) are also in that direction.
The Microbe (Y) arrow points in a different direction, so it's separate
from the hydrogel effect. The Fertilizer treatments group together, and
is also in the opposite direction to MicrobeY.

In examining the partitioning of the variance, these these factors
(hydrogel and microbe) are driving 23.9% of the multivariate response.
This is consistent with the PERMANOVA R2 above. Therefore, Hydrogel and
Microbe presence are meaningful predictors of soil physiochemical
properties (leachate, moisture, and wheat yield), but there are other
drivers for the remaining 75% of these multivariate responses.

### PCA

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
# Uses soil_properties_rel already built above
# scale = TRUE equalizes variance across variables (z-score equivalent)
soil_pca <- rda(soil_properties_rel, scale = TRUE)

# How much variance does each PC explain?
summary(soil_pca)

# Scree plot - where does variance flatten out?
screeplot(soil_pca, bstick = TRUE, type = "lines",
          main = "PCA Screeplot - Soil Properties")

# Extract proportion of variance for axis labels
pca_summary <- summary(soil_pca)
pc1_var <- round(pca_summary$cont$importance[2,1] * 100, 1)  # % variance PC1
pc2_var <- round(pca_summary$cont$importance[2,2] * 100, 1)  # % variance PC2

# Build scores data frame (same pattern as NMDS)
pca_scores <- vegan::scores(soil_pca, tidy = TRUE) |>
  filter(score == "sites") |>
  left_join(cluster_df, by = "label")

# Extract species (variable) scores for arrows
pca_arrows <- vegan::scores(soil_pca, display = "species") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("variable")

# Plot
p_pca <- ggplot(pca_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = treatment_colors, name = "Treatment Group") +
  # Add variable arrows
  geom_segment(data = pca_arrows,
               aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")),
               color = "darkgray", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_text(data = pca_arrows,
            aes(x = PC1 * 1.15, y = PC2 * 1.15, label = variable),
            color = "darkgray", size = 3, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = cluster), level = 0.95, 
               linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", pc1_var, "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", pc2_var, "%)"),
       caption = "Figure 5: PCA of Soil Physiochemical Properties and Wheat Yield")

p_pca
```

## Soil ions

### PERMANOVA

I will use the same PERMANOVA approach using these treatment categories:

1.  T3 - BioBead - bacteria, AMF
2.  T9 - Liquid consortia
3.  T11 - Empty bead

The hypothesis is that there are differences in soil ion supply rates
for these different treatment groups. To do this, I will filter the
dataset and make a new distance matrix. Same as above, the permutations
not restricted, as the study utilized a randomized block design so there
are no bench effects to account for.

```{r}
# PERMANOVA
set.seed(1)
ion_permanova_result <- adonis2(ions_dist ~ ions_treatments, 
                                permutations = 9999)
ion_permanova_result
```

<!--# update this section -->

In this test, the treatment group explained 59.7% of the multivariate
variance (R² = 0.59729), with a highly significant F statistic (F =
4.4496, p = 0.0037). This confirms the hypothesis that there are
differences in soil ion supply rate in these different treatment groups.

Practically, these data mean that the 3 treatment groups produce
meaningfully different multivariate ion supply rates. Like in the soil
physiochemical profile above, these three treatments isolate the carrier
and microbial effects, so the separation suggests the hydrogel carrier
and microbial consortia are each contributing something distinct rather
than being interchangeable.

### Two-Factor PERMANOVA

Using the same data modification approach in the previous section, I
coded each treatment in the ion dataset with a Hydrogel Y/N and a
Microbe Y/N for a Two-Factor ANOVA.

```{r}
ion_gel2factor <- read.csv("ions/PRS_2025_gel2factor.csv", header = TRUE, row.names = 1)

# Subset 
ion_properties <- ion_gel2factor[ , !colnames(ion_gel2factor) %in% 
                                    c("Treatment_Category", "Hydrogel", "Microbe")]

# Relativize/redo distance matrix
ion_properties_rel <- decostand(ion_properties, method = "max")
ion2factor_dist <- vegdist(ion_properties_rel, method = "euclidean")

set.seed(1)
ion_permanova_2way <- adonis2(
  ion2factor_dist ~ Hydrogel * Microbe,
  data = ion_gel2factor,
  permutations = 9999,
  by = "term"
)
ion_permanova_2way
```

<!--# More SS analysis-->

Similar to the other multivariate responses in the previous section, the
hydrogel accounts for only 6.7% of the variance in the responses (F =
1.8652, p = 0.0908). But this result is not statistically significant.
The presence or absence of microbe accounts for 14.4% of the variance
and is very significant (F = 3.5212, p = 0.0070). Together, their
interaction accounts for 8.6% of the variance and is borderline
statistically significant (F = 2.1102, p = 0.0613). So the presence of
the hydrogel is not significant in terms of its impacts on the soil ion
supply rate. It is worth noting that there are fewer sample units
compared to soil physiochemical properties (42 instead of 98), so the
lack of significance may be a result of a comparatively under-powered
test.

### RDA

```{r}
ion_rda <- rda(
  ion_properties_rel ~ Hydrogel * Microbe,
  data = ion_gel2factor,
  scale = FALSE  
)
summary(ion_rda)

# Significance test of the full model
set.seed(1)
anova(ion_rda, permutations = 9999)
anova(ion_rda, by = "term", permutations = 9999)

# Plot (run together)
plot(ion_rda, type = "n")
points(ion_rda, display = "sites", 
       col = treatment_colors[ion_gel2factor$Treatment_Category], 
       pch = 16, cex = 1.2)
text(ion_rda, display = "bp", col = "#1927DDFF")  # arrows for explanatory variables
legend("bottomleft", legend = names(treatment_colors), 
       col = treatment_colors, pch = 16, cex = 0.7)
mtext("Figure 4: RDA of Soil Ion Supply Rate constrained by Hydrogel and Microbe presence", 
      side = 1, # bottom of plot
      line = 4, # how far below the axis
      cex = 0.8) # font size
```

<!--# Update this section-->

In examining the breakdowns of the RDA axes, RDA1 explains 9.7% of the
variation (F = 2.1324, p = 0.0062) and there is a nice separation of
treatments along this axis. RDA2 picks up another 3.6%, and RDA3 another
1.2%. There is still significant variation found in the unconstrained
axes (\~86%) that is not explained by Hydrogel or Microbe factors.

The arrows for Hydrogel and Microbe are pointing in similar directions,
meaning that these explanatory variables are correlated with each other
and driving similar patterns in the ion supply rate responses. It is
worth noting that treatments that have microbes but no hydrogel are few
in this data set (Liquid_Mixed, HardyGro). As a result of this design,
it may be difficult to complelety detangle these factors. It could be
worthwhile to remove some lower priority treatment categories like
HalfFert_HalfBB, BB_Mixed_Reduced to balance the analysis for a cleaner
interpretation.

The proportion of constrained variance is 0.1441 or 14.41%, meaning that
Hydrogel + Microbe and their interactions account for 14% of the
variation in response of this system. This is higher than 10.7% with the
leachate, moisture, and wheat yield responses in the previous section.
So these factors are having a stronger influence on soil ion dynamics
than these other response variables. It makes biological sense that
microbial activity and hydrogel water retention would have more direct
effects on ion exchange at the root zone than on other metrics.

The ion data in general may be telling a cleaner story. The PRS probes
are gathering ion exchange near the rhizosphere over a 2-week period. It
is closer to the nutrient exchange occuring between microbes and plant
roots than leachate, moisture, and wheat yield.

### PCA

```{r}
# Uses soil_properties_rel already built above
# scale = TRUE equalizes variance across variables (z-score equivalent)
ion_pca <- rda(ion_properties_rel, scale = TRUE)

# How much variance does each PC explain?
summary(ion_pca)

# Scree plot - where does variance flatten out?
screeplot(ion_pca, bstick = TRUE, type = "lines",
          main = "PCA Screeplot - Ion Properties")

# Extract proportion of variance for axis labels
ionpca_summary <- summary(ion_pca)
ionpc1_var <- round(ionpca_summary$cont$importance[2,1] * 100, 1)  # % variance PC1
ionpc2_var <- round(ionpca_summary$cont$importance[2,2] * 100, 1)  # % variance PC2

cluster_df_ions <- data.frame(
  label = rownames(ion_properties_rel),
  cluster = as.factor(ion_gel2factor$Treatment_Category)
)

# Build scores data frame (same pattern as NMDS)
ionpca_scores <- vegan::scores(ion_pca, tidy = TRUE) |>
  filter(score == "sites") |>
  left_join(cluster_df_ions, by = "label")

# Extract species (variable) scores for arrows
ionpca_arrows <- vegan::scores(ion_pca, display = "species") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("variable")

# Plot
ionp_pca <- ggplot(ionpca_scores, aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, colour = cluster)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_color_manual(values = treatment_colors, name = "Treatment Group") +
  # Add variable arrows
  geom_segment(data = ionpca_arrows,
               aes(x = 0, y = 0, xend = PC1, yend = PC2),
               arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2, "cm")),
               color = "darkgray", inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_text(data = ionpca_arrows,
            aes(x = PC1 * 1.15, y = PC2 * 1.15, label = variable),
            color = "darkgray", size = 3, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  stat_ellipse(aes(group = cluster), level = 0.95, 
               linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.4) +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.text = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = paste0("PC1 (", ionpc1_var, "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", ionpc2_var, "%)"),
       caption = "Figure 6: PCA of Soil Ion Supply Rate")

ionp_pca
```
